title: The Chef of the Century
tagline: He earned more Michelin stars than any chef in history — through obsession and perfection.

scenes.text: Paris, 1981. The restaurant Jamin has been open for three years, and critics are already using words they reserve for once-in-a-generation events. The chef is 35 years old. He will go on to earn 32 Michelin stars — more than any human being in history.

scenes.speaker: Joël Robuchon
scenes.text: I make the best mashed potato in the world. People laugh when I say this. But equal weight of butter to potato, passed through a fine sieve, seasoned with precision — there is nothing more technically demanding in cooking. Perfecting the simple is harder than anything complex.

challenge.instruction: Perfecting the simple is the hardest thing in cooking. Make Robuchon's mashed potatoes the Jamin way, every step in its place.
challenge.fact: At his peak, Joël Robuchon held 32 Michelin stars across his restaurants worldwide — more than any chef in history. His empire spanned Paris, Monte Carlo, Las Vegas, Tokyo, Hong Kong, and beyond, each kitchen reflecting his obsessive pursuit of perfection.

scenes.text: The Gault Millau guide named Robuchon 'Chef of the Century' in 1989. At 51, exhausted, he retired — an almost unheard-of act in the world of grand cuisine. He gave up everything, vanished from the kitchen. Then, years later, he came back with an entirely new concept.

scenes.speaker: Food Critic
scenes.text: Monsieur Robuchon — why did you retire at the height of your powers? And why come back with these small counter-seats, this informal style? It is so different from your three-star formality.

challenge.instruction: Robuchon answers the critic with a counter, not a speech. Take L'Atelier from Saint-Germain round the world and finish the season ahead of the rival houses.
challenge.fact: Robuchon's retirement in 1996 was unprecedented in fine dining. He said he was exhausted and wanted to explore life beyond the kitchen. Seven years later, his return with the L'Atelier concept — casual counter seating around an open kitchen — reinvented fine dining for a new generation.

scenes.speaker: Joël Robuchon
scenes.text: I retired because I was dying inside. Haute cuisine had become theater — elaborate, cold, and distant. I came back with L'Atelier because I wanted to cook at a counter where I could see the guest's face. The best meal is the one you share close enough to talk.

challenge.instruction: L'Atelier puts the cooks behind a counter, in full view of the guests. Share the work along the counter so no station holds up the meal.
challenge.fact: Robuchon spent years studying Japanese culinary philosophy — the concept of shokunin kishitsu (craftsman's spirit) deeply influenced his cooking. His L'Atelier restaurants, modelled on Japanese counter dining, blended French technique with Japanese minimalism and obsessive attention to the guest experience.

scenes.text: Robuchon opened L'Atelier restaurants in Paris, Tokyo, Las Vegas, London, and Hong Kong. Every one earned Michelin stars. He trained a generation of chefs — including Gordon Ramsay — and changed the vocabulary of fine dining from performance to intimacy.

challenge.instruction: Robuchon's kitchens now run on three continents, and he calls them all. Work out the time in each city before the phone rings.
challenge.fact: When Robuchon died in 2018, his restaurants around the world held 31 Michelin stars between them — more than any other chef.

scenes.speaker: Joël Robuchon
scenes.text: A recipe is only a beginning. The real ingredient is attention — attention to the product, attention to the fire, attention to the person who will eat what you have made. Every plate is a letter. Make sure it says something true.

challenge.instruction: Every plate is a letter, and every one must say something true. Line up the ingredients at the pass until each plate is perfect.
challenge.fact: This is one of the most misunderstood facts about the Michelin system. Stars belong to the restaurant address and experience, not the individual chef. When Robuchon retired and closed his restaurants, their stars vanished. When he returned with L'Atelier, he earned new stars from scratch — accumulating more than any chef in history.

scenes.speaker: Joël Robuchon
scenes.text: Diego Maradona and Michael Jackson are still in the rival's hand; they will come to the board one by one. Follow them, start the Tech Race where they stand, and fight with Kill mode on. A player with no Great People left is out of the game.

challenge.instruction: Fight lesson 7 · Conquest. Deploy, move to wherever the rival stands, start the Tech Race there, and attack with Kill mode on until the rival has no Great People left.
challenge.fact: With Kill mode on, a beaten card is discarded instead of returning to hand. A player with no Great People left, in hand or on the board, is out, and the last player standing wins. A kill won in a Great Person's own stat also counts towards their achievement.
